links.why: Before each move in chess you think what happens next, and that is how you solve problems.
The chess board is a square grid, and each piece moves in its own shape of path, straight or diagonal.
In chess each piece is worth some points, so you can add up who is ahead.
Chess began in India long ago, and it was called chaturanga.
The rook goes straight and the bishop goes diagonal, so you are using directions on a map.
In a chess class you plan a few moves ahead, which is how to solve any hard problem.
Good players spot the same patterns again and again, like a fork or a trap.
Chess started in India as chaturanga, and it travelled across the world.
Each piece moves along rows, columns or diagonals, like following directions on a map.
When your finger flicks the striker, it pushes the coin and the coin changes direction.
The powder on the board lets the striker slide far because it reduces friction.
The striker keeps moving until it hits a coin or the edge, because moving things keep moving.
Each coin has points, so you add them up to find the score.
You aim at angles and bounce off the sides, so you are using shapes and angles.
You count each square as you move your token the number the dice shows.
You add the dice number to your place, so you can say where you will land.
If you roll the dice many times, you can count how often each number comes and show it as a graph.
Playing together means you listen to the rules and take turns to speak.
The board has numbers from 1 to 100, so you read them in order as you go.
Each throw you add the dice number, and a ladder adds a jump while a snake takes you back.
This game started in India long ago as a way to teach right and wrong, and it was called Moksha Patam.
The numbers on the board go in rows that change direction, which is a pattern you can see.
Each card has a number and you put them in order, from the smallest to the biggest.
In many card games you add up the numbers in your hand.
You can sort cards by suit and count each group, then show it in a table.
You have to remember which cards were played and guess what the others hold.
Each piece fits only where its edges match, so you turn and flip shapes in your head.
Finding the edges first and then sorting by colour is a way of solving a big problem in small steps.
You look for a repeating colour or line to know which pieces go next to each other.
You can count the pieces, then count how many are still left.
A riddle has an answer hidden in it, and you find it by trying ideas one by one.
Crosswords and riddles make you find the right word for a clue.
A paheli plays with words, so you learn new Hindi words and what they mean.
Sudoku and number puzzles follow a pattern, and you find which number fits.
Each block has a shape, and you see how they fit together to make a bigger shape.
You count the studs and the blocks, and you can see two rows of four make eight.
A block with 2 rows of 4 studs has 2 times 4, which is 8 studs.
Blocks are made of strong plastic or wood because they must not break when pressed together.
You push the blocks together and pull them apart, and both are forces.
The tower falls when it leans too far, because gravity pulls everything down.
Your hand pushes each block into place, and a small push can make the tower fall.
You can measure how tall the tower is with a ruler or by counting blocks.
Try a wide base and then a narrow base and see which tower stays up longer.
You solve the cube by learning small steps in order and repeating them.
You turn a cube in your mind and picture how it looks from the other sides.
Each move set is a pattern you repeat, and the colours come back in order.
Many children time themselves with a stopwatch and see their seconds go down.
In a game like Business you pay, earn and give change with play money.
You add the dice and add or take away money as you play.
Word games like Scrabble help you learn new words and how to spell them.
Every game has rules that everyone follows, so the game is fair.
You pick up seeds and drop them one by one in each cup, so you count a lot.
Sharing seeds into cups is like dividing them into equal groups.
These seed games are very old and children have played them in India for hundreds of years.
The same game has different names in Tamil, Telugu and Kannada, and in other places.
When you play doctor or teacher, you learn what people in that job do.
In pretend play you speak in someone else's voice and listen to the others.
Playing house shows how a family shares work and looks after each other.
Playing shop, you use pretend money and give change.
In a toy shop you add prices and give change back.
A shopkeeper buys things and sells them for a bit more, and that is how a shop earns.
A shopkeeper weighs rice and dal in kilos and grams, and you can do it with your toy scale.
You add up what the customer bought and take away what they paid.
The roof sags and falls without a chair or a stack of books to hold it up, because gravity pulls it down.
A bedsheet is light and bendy, so it makes a good roof, but a cushion is soft and good for walls.
Inside a thick blanket fort it is dark, because the blanket blocks the light.
You think of how to make a room with walls and a roof from flat pieces.
Cardboard is light, bendable and strong when folded, and you can test that.
Cardboard comes from trees, made of paper that is pressed in layers.
Using an old box again means less goes to waste.
You measure and cut the sides so the box fits together.
When you read a story, you see who is in it, where it is and what happens.
A story book has words you do not know yet, and you can guess them from the story.
Writers use words to show how a place looks, sounds and feels.
After you read, you can tell or write what happened in your own words.
When you read a Hindi kahani, you see what happens to each character.
Reading shows you new Hindi words, and you can ask what they mean.
Many old stories from India carry lessons about how to live well.
Panchatantra stories have clever animals, and you can ask what real animals do.
In a comic the story is told by pictures and words together.
You can read the speech bubbles out loud in different voices.
Amar Chitra Katha tells stories about people from the past, and you can find out when they lived.
You can draw your own comic and write one sentence in each box.
When you tell a story, you plan what comes first, next and last, and say it clearly.
You can tell a story in Hindi or your home language, and others listen.
Grandparents' stories carry what the family remembers from long ago.
A story told out loud can be written down with a beginning, middle and end.
Rhymes sound alike at the end, like cat and hat.
In antakshari you take the last letter of a song and start the next one with it.
Word games make you think of new words that start with a sound.
When you say a tongue twister, your voice box vibrates to make the sound.
A nature film shows how animals live, eat and look after their young.
In a documentary you can spot how a living thing is made for its place.
After a film, you can tell someone one new thing you learned.
A space film shows the planets and the Sun, as far as telescopes can see.
You can describe what you saw in the film using exact words.
After a cartoon, you can tell what happened and what you thought of it.
A cartoon story has a beginning, a problem and an end, like a story book.
The screen shows pictures that change fast, and your eyes see them as moving.
Taking breaks from the screen and sitting away from it keeps your eyes safe.
After a film, you can tell your friends what you liked and why.
Loud cinema sound can hurt ears, so we sit back and protect our hearing.
The cinema is dark so that the light from the screen is the only one we see.
India makes films in many languages, such as Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and Hindi.
A video call keeps you close to family who live far away.
You can find on a map where your grandparents live and how far away it is.
When one place is far away, the time can differ, so you check when to call.
On a call you wait for your turn to speak and listen to the answer.
Your voice is sent as a signal and a speaker makes the vibration again at the other end.
In coding you break a big job into small steps and test each one.
To make a robot turn left or move forward, you give it directions.
A loop repeats the same steps again and again, which is a pattern.
Drawing a square in Scratch uses four equal sides and four turns.
A robot toy works because electricity goes round a complete loop inside it.
A magician makes you look at one hand while the other does the trick, because our eyes can only focus on one place.
A good magician talks while performing and keeps the audience interested.
Many number tricks work because of a pattern the magician knows.
Some tricks use a hidden magnet that pulls iron without touching it.
Once you know how the trick works, you can test it again and again to be sure.
A spinning top stays up because spinning keeps it from falling over.
The top slows down because the floor and the air rub against it.
The pull of your string puts energy into the top, and it spends it as it spins.
You can time how many seconds the top spins and compare each try.
When your marble hits another, it passes on its push and the other goes away.
A marble rolls on until something stops it, like friction or another marble.
Players measure how far each marble went to see who won.
You count the marbles you won and the ones you lost.
The danda hits the gilli and pushes it up and away.
The score is how far the gilli flew, which you measure in danda lengths.
This is one of the oldest street games of India, played for hundreds of years.
The hit changes the gilli from still to fast, and gravity then brings it down.
The seeker counts to a number out loud while the others hide.
You describe where you hid, such as behind, under or next to the door.
Everyone agrees on the limits of the game so no one goes somewhere unsafe.
You can hide behind something opaque but not behind a glass window.
Tic-tac-toe is played on a grid, and you think about which rows can make three in a line.
You think what the other player will do next and block them.
Hangman and name place animal thing need you to think of words and spell them.
In dots and boxes you count and add the boxes each player has closed.
A paper plane glides because its wings push the air down and the air pushes it up.
When you fold paper in half, both sides match, which is symmetry.
A fold line is a line of symmetry and both halves look the same.
Change only the wing shape and see which plane flies farthest.
A paper boat floats because it is light and water holds it up.
The wind lifts the kite up, and without wind it comes down.
A kite stays up because the air pushes against its flat face and pushes it up.
Many kites are diamonds with two matching halves.
Kites fill the sky at Makar Sankranti and Uttarayan in Gujarat.
Sharp manja can cut hands and birds, so we use plain thread and fly in open spaces.
A car goes farther on a smooth floor than on a rug, because of friction.
You push a car to start it, and the harder you push the faster it goes.
Use the same ramp and change only the floor, and you can compare fairly.
You can measure how far each car rolled after the ramp.
Toy trains and cars show how real vehicles carry people and goods.
The ball rolls down because gravity pulls it down the slope.
A ramp is a simple machine, because it helps you lift a load with a small push.
Make the ramp higher and see if the ball goes farther.
You mark where the ball stopped and measure the distance from the ramp.
Many games set a puzzle and you try different plans until one works.
In a game you find your way using a map and directions like left and right.
Setting a timer for game time teaches you how long half an hour is.
We keep to screen time limits and never share our name or address with strangers online.
Looking at a screen for too long makes eyes tired, so we look far away from time to time.
A spelling bee makes you learn how words are made of letters.
In a quiz you listen carefully to the whole question before you answer.
Quiz questions often ask about states, capitals and languages of India.
You can find a place from a quiz question on a map.
You follow clues like go ten steps forward and turn left.
A treasure map shows places and which way to go, like a real map.
Each clue leads to the next, so you think step by step.
You can measure the steps from one place to another.
A balloon gets big because you fill it with air, and air takes up space.
Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall, because of static charge.
When you let go of a blown balloon, the air rushes out and pushes the balloon the other way.
You can count how many balloons for each child and share them equally.
A bubble is a thin skin of soapy water holding air inside.
The colours that you see on a bubble come from light bouncing off the thin skin.
Bubbles are always round, no matter what shape the wand is.
A bubble floats along on the wind, and you can see which way the air moves.
A shadow forms because your hand is opaque and blocks the light.
Light moves in straight lines, so the shadow has the same shape as your hand.
Kathputli and Tholu Bommalata are old puppet arts of Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh.
In a puppet show you speak in a different voice for each character.
One domino falls and pushes the next, so the push passes along the line.
The dominoes fall down because gravity pulls them to the floor.
You line them up in a pattern, and you can count in twos or fives.
Energy is passed from one domino to the next down the line.
In an experiment you change one thing and keep everything else the same.
A magnifying glass is a lens, and it bends light to make things look bigger.
You measure each time so you can compare your results.
You write down what you saw and draw a graph to compare.
Hit the drum and the skin shakes, and shaking makes the sound.
A tune has a pattern of long and short notes that repeats.
Loud toys can hurt your ears, so keep the sound low.
Pachisi, chaupar and aadu puli were played in India long ago, and some are still played.
In games like aadu puli, you decide which way to move to trap the other.
You count steps for your tokens around the board.
Playing together with grandparents and cousins brings the family close.
Housie asks you to hear the number and find it on your ticket.
Add two dice together and you get a number from 2 to 12.
Roll a dice 30 times and count how many of each number, and see which comes up most.
Multiply the two dice numbers and see which pairs make the same answer.
You remember where the pairs are by seeing where they were turned over before.
Your eyes see the card and your brain keeps it for a while, so the game trains your memory.
You can describe each picture in words to help yourself remember it.
A good plan, like going row by row, helps you do better.
Wet sand holds a shape and dry sand does not, so materials behave differently.
Sand does not dissolve in water, but it mixes with it into a muddy mixture.
You can sort what you find into soft, hard, rough and smooth.
You mould shapes like balls, cylinders and cubes.
You count your jumps and try to beat your last number.
A rope swings round again and again, just like a pendulum, in the same time.
Hopscotch has a pattern of single and double squares to hop.
After jumping your heart beats faster and you breathe harder.
